summary: Hands-on SDK integration lab for Python and TypeScript clients. Walked through API keys vs KMS-backed credentials, quickstart repo, environment variables, and a private sandbox setup with VPC peering. Discussed perf targets and next steps to run a short POC benchmark. Security team asked about audit logs and key rotation; Redwood to follow up with docs.
topics: Auth patterns: API key vs KMS/HSM + rotation
Environment setup: sandbox, VPC peering, egress rules
Console quickstart and sample repo overview
transcript:
[00:00] Lina: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um this is Lina from Redwood, I think we have about 50 minutes so we'll do a quick alignment then jump into a live walk through of the sample repo and auth patterns.
[01:12] Priya: Hey hi, yeah thanks. we care about two things mainly: latency under 100ms for our search autocomplete and no customer data leaving our VPC, so the KMS route is important.
[02:05] Marcus: cool, we'll show both: simple API key for dev and the KMS-backed flow for private. note that the KMS flow requires a small agent in your network or a temp credential exchange.
[04:20] Tom: quick q — the quickstart repo, does it include the typescript example for streaming? last call i saw it but wanted to confirm.
[05:05] Lina: yes, there's a streaming example and a small python script that runs a tokenized throughput test. we'll open the repo now.
[06:50] Devon: i might interrupt — our security lead Sara asked about log retention, is that handled in the private deploy or console level?
[07:30] Sara: yes, we need audit logs for 1 year and key rotation schedule. also need proof of SOC2 controls.
[08:40] Marcus: on private deployments you can push logs to your SIEM, retention is customer controlled. for hosted we retain default 90 days but enterprise add-on supports longer. i'll put links in follow up.
[10:15] Priya: ok let's go through the python flow.
[11:00] Marcus: so first step pip install redwood-client, set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env or for k m s flow run the helper that exchanges a signed JWT for a short lived token. code snippet: from redwood import Client - client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) — note: that's pseudocode.
[13:42] Priya: i noticed the helper is using workload identity: can it integrate with our GCP workload identity federation?
[14:10] Marcus: yes we have examples for GCP workload identity and AWS STS, also a step-by-step for onprem HSM via our connector. it does require a lightweight sidecar for caching keys.
[16:00] Tom: how is kv cache handled for repeated prompts? we want to avoid repeat token costs for our autocomplete.
[16:40] Lina: we support prefix caching and server side kv cache pinning — you can configure cache TTL per route. on dedicated/dedicated-private you can pin across pods.
[18:55] Priya: any gotchas about environment variables? we rotate keys nightly and have CI that injects secrets.
[19:30] Marcus: our SDK supports reading from common secret managers and also from env var fallback. for CI you can set REDWOOD_API_KEY as a secret and the quickstart includes a github actions step.
[21:05] Devon: let's demo the typescript quickstart now.
[21:40] Marcus: opening the ts example: yarn install, create .env.local with REDWOOD_API_KEY or use KMS helper. here's the streaming example using EventSource — note sometimes browsers block chunked streams behind certain proxies, we include a server-sse proxy in the repo.
[24:10] Tom: we run behind an internal proxy with mTLS — will that block streaming?
[24:45] Marcus: streaming requires either websocket or SSE; for proxies that buffer you can use our chunked polling fallback. latency suffers but it keeps compatibility.
[27:00] Priya: what about per-route quotas? we need to throttle only the autocomplete route.
[27:30] Lina: you can set per-route quotas in console and attach model variants per route. we demo that in the console quickstart.
[29:10] Marcus: also showed Optimize suggestions: batching and quantization recommendations based on observed payloads. but for low-latency autocomplete you likely disable heavy batching.
[31:00] Sara: please clarify data residency — we are required to ensure no PII leaves region.
[31:35] Lina: for private you can deploy in your VPC or on-prem, that keeps data local. for hosted we offer region pinning and data retention controls. we'll send the data residency whitepaper.
[33:50] Priya: let's try a live run — Marcus run the python micro-benchmark with the seed dataset Verdant provided.
[34:10] Marcus: starting the script now, it's sending 200 short prompts at concurrency 8.
[36:30] Marcus: results so far: p50 = 78ms, p95 = 230ms, note p95 spikes during cold KV cache miss.
[37:10] Tom: ok p95 is high, can you reproduce split by model variant?
[37:45] Marcus: switching to a trimmed quantized variant — rerunning.
[40:10] Marcus: new run p50 = 85ms p95 = 160ms, cost per token dropped ~35%. this is typical tradeoff.
[41:30] Priya: good, but we need to validate with our full payloads and concurrency growth to 50c.
[42:05] Lina: agreed, that's the POC scope. we'll run a bench with your payload and suggested routing policies.
[43:20] Sara: about audit logs — if we go dedicated can we push logs to our Splunk instance?
[44:00] Marcus: yes we support pushing via syslog/HTTPS. will include config snippet in follow up.
[45:10] Devon: what's the expected timeline to spin up the private sandbox?
[45:35] Lina: we can provision a sandbox with VPC peering in 3-5 business days once we have CIDR and KMS policy.
[47:05] Tom: how does billing look for the sandbox? we prefer a usage-only test for POC.
[47:30] Lina: sandboxes can be usage-based, we'll send pricing tiers; dedicated commitments start monthly.
[48:50] Priya: ok final recap please.
[49:05] Lina: recap: we'll send KMS setup guide, sample repo link, benchmark script; Marcus will provision sandbox after CIDR; Verdant will confirm KMS policy and retention. next meeting to run full POC bench scheduled for 2025-04-11.
[51:10] Sara: thanks all.
[51:35] Marcus: thanks, i'll follow up with the links.
[52:00] Meeting end.
